Share Analyzer Report
Application report · Testing phase

Share Analyzer

A transparent, weight-based research tool for Indian shares and IPOs

“Share Analyzer” is a working name. The final name will change in a future release. The application is in a testing phase and does not claim to be 100% correct; its views come from a weighted combination of scores set by adjustable weights and a bias. Nothing here is investment advice.

1Summary

Share Analyzer is a desktop application that helps an individual investor research a listed Indian share or an upcoming IPO in one place. You type a company name. The application then reads international news, Indian news and the company’s own news, checks its growth, latest results, valuation, market mood, chart levels and upcoming events, and finishes with a BUY, HOLD or SELL view for three holding periods: short term (1–2 weeks), mid term (1–6 months) and long term (6 months or more).

The application is built around one idea: every step is visible. Each of the 43 factors gives a score from −10 to +10, each has a weight, and the final view is a weighted average of those scores. The user can see every score, change every weight, and add a personal bias. Nothing is hidden inside a model that cannot be explained.

5,526listed shares covered (NSE main board, NSE SME, BSE)
43share factors in 10 groups, each scored −10 to +10
3separate views: short, mid and long term
~100filter choices in Share search

Beyond single-share analysis, the application includes an IPO page (main-board and SME issues with grey-market premium, subscription and a listing-day and long-term view), the exchanges’ ASM / GSM surveillance lists, a Share search screener with nearly 100 filter choices, a portfolio with live prices, today’s gain or loss and a capital-gains tax estimate, and a small weather and season factor that applies only to weather-sensitive businesses.

Status of this report

The application is in a testing phase. Figures and screenshots in this report come from the testing version on 9–12 October 2026 and are shown only to explain how the application works. They are not recommendations to buy or sell any security. The application does not claim to be 100% correct (see Section 14).

2What the application is, and what it is not

Share Analyzer is a personal research assistant. It collects public market information that an investor would otherwise gather from many websites, puts it in one consistent format, and applies a clear, adjustable scoring method to it.

It isIt is not
A research tool that runs on the user’s own computerA trading platform. It cannot place, modify or cancel any order
A transparent scoring method with visible weights and biasA black-box prediction engine
A way to compare many shares quickly and consistentlySEBI-registered investment advice
A testing-phase project that is being validatedA product that guarantees returns or accuracy

The application is written in Python (for the engine) and a plain web interface that opens in the user’s browser. It is fully portable: the whole application, including its own copy of Python, lives in one folder that can be copied to another Windows computer and started with a double-click on start.bat. No installation and no account are needed.

3How easy it is to use

The home screen has one search box. The user types a company name, a stock symbol or an IPO name in plain words, for example “HDFC”, “STL Tech” or “Orient Cables IPO”, and presses Enter. The application works out which listed company is meant, then shows its progress step by step while it works. A full analysis usually takes between 30 and 90 seconds, most of it spent reading news.

  • One box for everything. Shares and IPOs are typed into the same box; no codes or menus are required.
  • Plain-language results. Each result starts with an “In short” line and lists what is working for and against the share before showing any numbers.
  • Everything folds away. Long sections (results tables, headlines, court cases, related stocks) are collapsed until the user opens them, so the first screen stays short.
  • History. Every analysis is saved on the computer and listed on the left, so it can be reopened later without running it again.
  • Built-in help. Every number has a short explanation next to it, and every factor shows why it scored what it scored.

Two themes: light and dark

The application has a light theme and a dark theme, plus an automatic mode that follows the computer’s own setting. The user can also pick an accent colour for buttons and highlights. Profit is always green and loss always red, in both themes.

4Analysing a share: a worked example (HDFC Bank)

To show what a full analysis contains, this section follows one real run of the testing version for HDFC Bank Limited (NSE: HDFCBANK), carried out on 11 October 2026 using market data up to 9 October 2026. The figures are shown only to illustrate the interface.

The analysis runs in a fixed order, from the widest view to the narrowest: global events → India → the company → its growth → its latest quarter → its valuation → market mood → chart levels → upcoming events. Each step reports a one-line finding.

In this run the application found six live global events (the top one being US interest rates), one India-level headline linked to the company, and 80 company headlines over 30 days, four of them negative. It measured 3-year revenue growth of +26.9% a year and profit growth of +19.7% a year, a June 2026 quarter with revenue +4% and profit +19% year on year, and a P/E of 13.8. It then made five automatic weight changes (explained in Section 6) and produced three views.

Basic statistics, cash flow and key dates

Before any rating, the application shows the basic numbers an analyst would check first: market capitalisation, price, 52-week high and low, face value, equity capital, number of shares, book value per share, P/E, P/B, ROE and ROCE, dividend yield and net worth. Next to them are cash-flow checks (operating cash flow, free cash flow, cash flow compared with profit over three years, and the change in share count) and key dates such as the next results date. Every data item is time-stamped.

Detailed sections

Below the summary, the result lists detailed sections that open on a click: quarterly results (each cell shows the value and its change against the previous quarter and the same quarter last year), yearly results, cash flow, the full news scan, every headline used (each one can be clicked to check the original), court cases and hearings, related stocks side by side, opportunities in other themes created by today’s news, companies that could benefit from this company’s bad news, and the list of weights that were adjusted automatically.

About the court-case check

The application looks for court, tribunal and regulator matters in two places: news headlines from the last 12 months that name the company together with a court or regulator, and the company’s own exchange filings about litigation and orders. It groups them by forum (Supreme Court, High Courts, NCLT / NCLAT, SEBI / SAT, tax tribunals, ED / CBI and others) and marks each as ongoing or closed. Because there is no free, complete database of Indian court cases by company, it only reports what it found; it never claims that no case exists, and its reading of a headline is not a legal finding.

The outcome

The outcome shows a verdict for each horizon with its score and expected range, the headline (mid-term) plan, entry, stop-loss and target levels taken from the chart, and the estimated return on a chosen amount (₹10,000 by default). The line under the boxes explains how the range was calculated. For HDFC Bank the mid-term score of +9 fell inside the HOLD band (−10 to +10), so the plan reads “hold if you own it; add only above the breakout level; exit below the stop-loss.”

5What the application looks at

For every share the application gathers the following information from public sources. The list also shows what the user can look up directly.

AreaWhat is checked
International newsLive global events (interest rates, crude oil, wars, trade and tariffs, commodity prices) and how strongly each touches this company’s sector
National (India) newsGovernment policy and rules (duties, standards, PLI schemes), government projects and orders, sector-wide legal and regulatory news
Company newsHeadlines from the last 30 days, judged in context (the share’s own price reaction is compared with the index), management changes, promoter and insider trades, FII and mutual fund moves, orders and guidance
Court casesMatters before courts, tribunals and regulators found in 12 months of news and in the company’s own filings, marked ongoing or closed
Basic statisticsMarket cap, price, 52-week range, face value, book value, P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE, EBITDA and EBITDA margin, dividend yield, debt to equity, promoter holding
Growth and qualityRevenue and profit growth over 3 years, cash flow compared with profit, receivables and working capital, return on capital, debt, share dilution
Latest resultsLatest quarter revenue and profit against the same quarter last year, margin trend, quarter-on-quarter momentum
ValuationP/E against sector peers and against its own 5-year average, PEG ratio, P/B and EV/EBITDA, analyst target (discounted to remove optimism)
Market moodNIFTY today and its trend, sector trend, foreign and domestic institutional flows, India VIX (the market’s fear gauge)
Chart levelsSupport and resistance, RSI, MACD, volume and delivery percentage, free float and liquidity
EventsResults and record dates, dividends, buybacks, bonus issues, lock-in expiry and price against IPO price for new listings
Related companiesPeers in the same theme or sector and companies named in the same news, each with a quick score

News is read in three layers on purpose: global → national → company. A rate decision in the United States, a new import duty in India and an order win for the company are different kinds of news and are scored separately, so that one loud headline cannot dominate the result.

6How the BUY, HOLD or SELL view is calculated

This section explains the method in plain words first. The exact formulas are given in the boxes for readers who want them.

Step 1: score each factor

The application has 43 factors for shares, grouped into 10 groups. Each factor looks at one thing (for example “P/E against sector peers” or “quarter profit year on year”) and gives it a score between −10 (very negative) and +10 (very positive). Zero means neutral. If the data for a factor cannot be found, the factor is left out rather than guessed.

GroupFactorsDefault weightExamples
Global news38Global events hitting the sector, US markets and Fed, crude and commodities
India news310Policy and rules, government projects and orders, sector legal news
Company news & insiders618Company news, management, promoter trades, FII/MF moves, orders, red flags
Growth & quality7153-year revenue and profit growth, cash flow, return on capital, debt
Quarterly results410Quarter revenue and profit YoY, margin trend, momentum
Valuation514P/E vs peers and own history, PEG, P/B and EV/EBITDA, analyst target
Market mood48NIFTY today and trend, FII/DII flows, India VIX
Technicals513Support and resistance, RSI, MACD, volume and delivery, liquidity
Events & dividends59Upcoming events, dividend yield, buyback/bonus, lock-in expiry
Weather & season15Only for weather-sensitive businesses; zero for all others

Step 2: combine the scores with weights

Each factor has a weight that says how much it should count. The final score is the weighted average of the factor scores, stretched to a scale of −100 to +100. A personal bias can then be added: a positive bias leans towards buying, a negative bias towards caution.

Final score

Score = 10 × Σ ( wᵢ × sᵢ ) ÷ Σ wᵢ + bias

Confidence = weight of factors with data ÷ weight of all factors × 100%

sᵢ = score of factor i (−10 … +10); wᵢ = its weight. Only factors with data are counted.

Weights come in layers, applied in this order: the default weights above, then the chosen investor style (persona), then the user’s own custom weights and bias, then automatic adjustments for what is happening in the market today, and finally the holding-period profile.

Step 3: three holding periods

The same factor scores are combined three times with different emphasis. Chart signals and market mood matter most for a 1–2 week view; growth and valuation matter most for a view of 6 months or more. The table shows how each group’s weight is multiplied for each horizon.

GroupShort (1–2 weeks)Mid (1–6 months)Long (6 months +)
Global news×1.3×1.0×0.5
India news×1.4×1.1×0.9
Company news×1.4×1.1×0.9
Growth & quality×0.2×0.9×1.9
Quarterly results×0.6×1.3×0.8
Valuation×0.2×1.0×1.6
Market mood×1.8×0.7×0.2
Technicals×2.2×0.8×0.3
Events×1.4×0.9×0.6
Weather & season×0.5×1.3×0.9

Step 4: turn the score into a view

Each horizon has its own score bands. Short-term scores swing less than long-term ones, so the bands are narrower. The bands were set so that, on neutral data, roughly one share in five is a BUY and one in five a SELL.

ViewShort termMid termLong term
STRONG BUY22 and above30 and above35 and above
BUY8 to 2111 to 2913 to 34
HOLD−7 to 7−10 to 10−12 to 12
SELL−21 to −8−29 to −11−34 to −13
STRONG SELLbelow −21below −29below −34

For someone who already owns the share, the same view is shown as an action: STRONG BUY or BUY becomes add more, HOLD stays hold, SELL becomes reduce and STRONG SELL becomes exit.

Built-in safeguards

  • Market factors cannot decide alone. Global news and market mood together are limited to 30% of the weight actually used, so a good or bad day for the whole market cannot by itself turn a share into a BUY or SELL.
  • Not enough data, no call. If less than 45% of the company-specific weight has data (common for new listings and thinly covered companies), the view becomes “WATCH: not enough data” instead of BUY or SELL.
  • Red flags cap the view. If a serious red flag is found (for example fraud or serious legal news about the company), the view cannot be better than HOLD, whatever the score.
  • Low confidence is labelled. If less than 60% of the total weight has data, the view carries a “low confidence” label.
  • User rules. The user can add simple rules such as “if debt score is below −5, the view can be at most HOLD”.

Step 5: the estimated return range

The score is also turned into a rough return range for each horizon. A score of +100 is treated as an expected return of 30% a year, a score of zero as no expected change, and the width of the range comes from the share’s own price volatility over the past year. For mid and long term views, the analyst consensus target (after a 10% discount for analyst optimism) is blended in at 30% when at least three analysts cover the share.

Estimated return over a horizon of t years

Expected return μ = (Score ÷ 100) × 0.30 × t

Mid and long term: μ = 0.7 × μ + 0.3 × (0.9 × analyst target ÷ price − 1)

Range = μ ± 0.674 × σ × √t

σ = annual volatility from one year of daily price changes; 0.674 covers the middle ~50% of outcomes.

For HDFC Bank, the mid-term score of +9 gives about +2.6% a year; with 22% annual volatility over 1–6 months, the middle-50% range is about −5% to +11%, with +2.7% most likely. The application states plainly that these are statistical estimates, not promises.

Investor styles (personas) and personal weights

Different investors care about different things, so the application offers seven ready-made personas, each a set of weight changes and a bias: Balanced (the default), Conservative, Long-term value, Dividend seeker, Aggressive, Momentum trader, and IPO listing gain. A conservative investor, for example, gives more weight to debt, governance and valuation and has a bias of −6.

On top of the persona, the user can set every weight and the bias personally from the Weights & bias panel. Every change is saved and applied to all later analyses.

Move a group’s score or the bias and watch the three views change. The starting values are an example, not a real share. This is a simplified, group-level version of the method: every factor in a group is assumed to have the same score.

CautiousNeutralBuy-leaning

Automatic weight adjustments

When something unusual is happening, the application shifts weights for that analysis and lists every change with its reason. Examples: when the India VIX is 20 or higher (high market fear), market-mood factors count 1.4 times more; when a live global event (such as a crude oil shock) strongly touches the company’s sector, the related factors count more; when results are due within ten days, event risk counts more and the soon-to-be-stale quarter figures count less; just after fresh results, the quarterly factors count more. Multipliers are kept between 0.5 and 2.5, and the feature can be switched off. In the HDFC Bank example five such changes were made.

7Where machine learning is used

The application uses machine learning in two different ways. It is important to separate what already runs today from what is planned once enough results have been collected.

Used today: understanding news

Reading thousands of headlines is the part of the work best suited to machine learning. The application can use two free, pre-trained language models that run entirely on the user’s own computer:

ModelSizeWhat it does
FinBERT~440 MBReads a financial headline and classifies its tone as positive, negative or neutral, with a strength. It was trained on financial news, so it understands phrases such as “misses estimates” or “margin pressure”.
MiniLM sentence model~90 MBTurns text into numbers (vectors) so the application can tell whether a policy or global headline is really about this company’s products or sector, even when the exact words differ.

These models are optional. They are installed once (about 1 GB including the engine that runs them) and need no internet connection afterwards, no graphics card and no paid account. If they are not installed, the application falls back to a weighted word list with negation handling (“not”, “despite”, “fails to”) and keyword matching, and keeps working. The result always states which method was used; the HDFC Bank example used the word-list method.

A headline’s tone alone can mislead, so company news is also judged in context: the share’s own price reaction in the one to two days after the news, compared with the NIFTY, counts for half against the headline’s tone. Older news counts less; a headline five days old counts half as much as one from today.

Planned: learning the weights and bias from results

Today the default weights are set by judgement, informed by common practice in equity research, and the user can change them. The next step is to let the data set them. Every analysis is already saved with all 43 factor scores, the view and the price at that moment, so what the share did afterwards can be measured. Once enough months of results exist, the weights can be learned as follows:

  • Measure each factor’s usefulness. For each factor, measure how well its score ranked shares by what actually happened over the following period (its rank correlation with later returns, known as the information coefficient, IC).
  • Shrink towards the defaults. With little history, trust the hand-set weights; as months of results build up, move towards the measured weights. This protects against fitting noise.
  • Learn the bias by calibration. Fit the final score to the actual probability that the share went up, so that the bias corrects a score that is systematically too optimistic or too cautious.
  • Report probabilities, not only labels. A view could then read “BUY, 62% chance of beating the NIFTY over 3 months”.
  • Test only on unseen periods. Weights are learned on past months and tested on the months that followed (walk-forward testing), never on the same data, and the hit rate is shown openly.
Planned learning of weights and bias

Measured weight wᵢ* = max(0, ICᵢ), rescaled to the same total

Blended weight wᵢ = λ × wᵢ(default) + (1 − λ) × wᵢ*, where λ = 24 ÷ (24 + months of history)

Probability of rise P = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−(a + b × Score))

ICᵢ = rank correlation of factor i with later returns; a = learned bias; b = learned scale.

This approach keeps the method explainable: the user still sees one weight per factor and one bias, but the numbers are justified by measured results rather than by judgement alone. All of this can run on the user’s own computer, offline, using the saved history.

What machine learning does not do here

The application does not train a model to predict tomorrow’s price, and it does not trade. Learning is limited to how much each visible factor should count and how the final score should be calibrated.

8IPO analysis

The IPO page lists issues that are open now, upcoming and recently listed, with separate tabs for main-board and SME IPOs. For each issue it shows the price band, the grey-market premium (GMP) and its percentage, the estimated listing price, subscription, dates and the listing date. The GMP is read from several public trackers and the range of readings is shown, because a single GMP figure can be misleading.

An IPO analysis uses 12 factors of its own and gives two separate views: one for listing-day gain and one for holding 6–12 months after listing.

IPO factorWeightIPO factorWeight
GMP as % of price band20Fresh issue vs offer for sale6
Subscription (QIB / NII / retail)15Market mood6
Valuation vs listed peers12Anchor investors5
Financials12Sector and news5
GMP trend8Use of funds; promoter record4 + 4
Lead manager record3

The listing-day view gives extra weight to GMP, its trend and subscription; the long-term view gives extra weight to valuation, financials, the share of fresh money raised and the promoter’s record. SME IPOs carry a more cautious long-term bias. The possible views are APPLY, APPLY FOR LISTING GAIN ONLY, NEUTRAL / RISKY and AVOID. For IPOs that have already listed, the page shows the listing-day price and the change since then, so the earlier view can be checked against what happened. The application notes clearly that the GMP is an unofficial indicator.

9Share search: a screener with nearly 100 filters

Apart from analysing one share, the application can search all 5,526 listed shares to find those that match the user’s conditions. Everything is chosen from drop-down lists and boxes; no formulas need to be typed.

Filter typeChoices
Sector and industry22 sectors as defined by the exchange, each with its industries
Where it tradesNSE, BSE or both; main board, SME or both; large, mid or small company (by market value rank)
Themes21 themes including weather-sensitive, power and electricity, solar and green energy, railways, defence, fertilisers and farm inputs, textiles, pharma, banks, IT, auto, metals, cement, infrastructure, real estate, FMCG, chemicals, oil and gas, telecom, logistics
Numbers (30)Market cap, price, face value, traded value, net profit, profit growth, sales, sales growth, EBITDA, EBITDA margin, quarterly growth, 3-year growth, EPS, P/E, P/B, dividend yield, ROE, ROCE, debt to equity, promoter holding and its change, price change over 1 day, 1 week, 1, 3, 6 and 12 months, distance from the 52-week high
Safety checksLeave out shares on the ASM / GSM surveillance lists; leave out companies with court cases found

Each number can be set to “more than”, “less than”, “between” or “equal to”, and each shows how many shares have that number available. The search also accepts plain sentences such as “profitable railway companies with PE below 30”, which it turns into filters.

Example search

The example below looks for automobile companies with net profit above ₹500 crore, profit growth above 10%, sales above ₹500 crore, market cap above ₹300 crore, face value above ₹8, a one-year price rise above 10%, ROE above 3% and a dividend yield above 0.1%. Out of 5,526 shares, three matched, and the search took 18.8 milliseconds.

  • Ready-made screens with one click: monsoon winners, railway order book, power and electricity with good returns, debt-free small caps, near 52-week high, good value, fast growers and dividend payers.
  • Near misses: shares that fail exactly one condition are listed with what they missed by, so a slightly strict filter does not hide good candidates.
  • Saved screens and alerts: a search can be saved, and the application reports when a new share starts to match it.
  • Analyse from the list: any result can be sent straight to a full analysis with one click.

The share list and daily prices are refreshed from the exchanges’ own published files; company numbers are refreshed about once a week. The database lives on the user’s computer and fills itself in the background while the application is open.

10ASM / GSM surveillance list

The stock exchanges place some shares under extra watch because of unusual price moves, heavy swings or weak financials, under SEBI’s surveillance framework. Trading in these shares is restricted (for example 100% margin, a narrower price band, or trade-for-trade settlement). The application shows the current lists in plain language: long-term ASM, short-term ASM, GSM and ESM, with each stage explained and the date the share was added.

Surveillance also feeds into the ratings: a share in a higher ASM stage has its short-term view capped, and Stage IV caps both the short and mid-term views. Being on a list is treated as a caution, not as proof of wrongdoing.

11Weather and season factor

Some businesses depend on the weather: fertiliser, seed and tractor makers, crop-linked companies and rural consumer brands on the monsoon; air conditioner and cooling makers and power companies on summer heat; hydro-power on rainfall; construction on excess rain. The application reads seasonal data and turns it into a small factor that applies only to such businesses.

  • Monsoon (June to September): rainfall since 1 June in 16 major farming regions, compared with the same days over the last 10 years.
  • El Niño / La Niña: the latest Oceanic Niño Index, a widely used measure of Pacific ocean warming that is linked to weaker Indian monsoons.
  • Heat (March to June): the temperature forecast for nine large cities.

Each weather-sensitive company gets a score from −10 to +10 depending on its business type (heat helps a cooling company but hurts construction, for example). The factor has a deliberately light weight and counts for nothing for other companies, so it can nudge a view but rarely change it on its own.

12Portfolio

The portfolio page tracks the shares the user owns. Several portfolios can be kept (for example one per family member).

Adding shares

  • By hand: type the share name, quantity, average buying price and, optionally, the buying date, then click Add share.
  • From a broker file: most brokers let the user download a holdings statement as a CSV or Excel file. The application reads that file and adds all holdings at once. The user never gives the application a broker login.
  • Edit or delete in a separate window: choose a holding from the list and change or remove it.

What it shows

  • Live price and today’s gain or loss for each holding and for the whole portfolio, using the exchange’s official previous close.
  • Profit or loss in rupees and percent, value and share of the portfolio, and how long each share has been held (short or long term for tax).
  • The current view for each holding, with the date it was analysed, a reminder when the view is more than three days old, and a one-click re-analysis. “Analyse all” re-runs every holding.
  • Warnings when one share is more than 25% of the portfolio, one sector more than 40%, there are fewer than five holdings, or a holding is down more than 25% from its buying price.

Capital-gains tax estimate

The application estimates the tax that would be due if all holdings were sold today. Holdings kept longer than 365 days count as long term. Short-term losses are set off against long-term gains, the yearly long-term exemption is applied, and health and education cess is added.

ItemSetting used
Short-term capital gains (held 365 days or less)20%
Long-term capital gains (held more than 365 days)12.5% on gains above the exemption
Long-term exemption per financial year₹1,25,000
Health and education cess4% of the tax

All rates are settings that can be updated when the budget changes. The estimate leaves out securities transaction tax, surcharge, other income and losses carried forward, and is labelled as an estimate.

13Live prices

A bar at the top of every page shows the NIFTY 50 and BSE SENSEX with their change for the day. While the market is open, the NIFTY figure refreshes every few seconds and the SENSEX about once a minute; each update is marked with a brief pulse. When the market is closed, the bar says so and shows the last closing values. The bar can be minimised.

  • On an analysis page, the share price refreshes every 10 seconds during market hours, and can be refreshed by hand at any time.
  • On the portfolio page, prices refresh every 30 seconds during market hours, and only the figures that changed are redrawn, so the page stays smooth.
  • The day’s change is always measured from the exchange’s official previous close, so a missing day in a price history cannot produce a wrong daily percentage.

Prices from free public feeds can be delayed by a few seconds to a few minutes. Where a fallback source is used, the bar labels it as delayed.

14Privacy and safety

The application was designed so that using it carries no risk to the user’s money or accounts.

ConcernHow it is handled
Broker accountsThe application never connects to Zerodha Kite, Groww, Upstox or any other broker. It never asks for a broker login, password, PIN or API key. Holdings are typed in or read from a file the user downloads.
TradingIt cannot place, change or cancel orders. It only reads public market information.
Personal dataPortfolios, saved searches, settings and past analyses are stored only in the application’s own folder on the user’s computer. Nothing is uploaded to any server, and no account or sign-up is needed.
PaymentsNo payment details are asked for or stored. The machine-learning models are free and run offline.
Internet useThe internet is used only to read public prices, news, exchange files and company figures. With the demo mode, the application can be tried with no market connection at all.
PortabilityThe whole application, including its own Python, sits in one folder. A clean copy for another computer starts with no portfolio, no history and no personal settings.
Use of dataPublic market data is used for personal research only; it is not resold or redistributed.

15Limitations and disclaimer

Share Analyzer does not claim to be 100% correct. Its views come from a weighted combination of scores, set by weights and a bias. Weights and bias are judgements, not laws of nature: two reasonable people can set them differently and get different views for the same share.

  • Testing phase. The method has not yet been validated over a full market cycle. The planned walk-forward testing (Section 7) is the way its accuracy will be measured and published.
  • Data quality. Free public data can be late, incomplete or wrong. The application leaves out missing data instead of guessing and shows confidence and coverage, but it cannot fix errors in the sources.
  • News reading is imperfect. Word lists and language models can misread sarcasm, mixed headlines or news about a different company with a similar name.
  • Court-case reporting is incomplete. It shows only what was found in news and filings, and an automated reading of a headline is not a legal finding.
  • Markets change. Relationships that held in the past (for example between valuation and later returns) may weaken or reverse.
  • Estimates are ranges, not promises. The return range covers only the middle half of likely outcomes; actual results can fall outside it.
Disclaimer

Share Analyzer is a personal research and education tool. It is not registered with SEBI as an investment adviser or research analyst, and nothing it shows is investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security. Grey-market premiums are unofficial. Users should verify all information independently and consult a registered adviser before investing.

16Next steps

  • Track record: show, for every past view, what the share actually did afterwards, and publish the hit rate by horizon and by view.
  • Learned weights and calibrated bias, as described in Section 7, with probabilities shown next to each view.
  • Watchlist with alerts when a view changes or a price level is crossed.
  • Comparison and export: compare shares side by side and export an analysis as a PDF.
  • Risk profile questionnaire to suggest a persona that fits the user.
  • A final name and a public release after testing.

Feedback from economists and market practitioners on the factor list, the default weights and the validation plan is especially welcome.
